summary: Representative Niagara system patterns that connect Epic sample materials to emitter structure, renderers, timing, and user parameters.

archetypes.intent: Build a readable one-shot explosion from separate flash, streamer, sprite body, debris, spark debris, post-process, decal, and ground dust layers.
core_graph_or_stack: Use multiple emitters, each with one visual job.
Sprite body owns pyro volume; debris mesh renderer owns physical chunks; decal owns surface evidence.
Color user parameters expose art direction without editing internal emitters.
Burst plus short sustain modules create impact first and residual motion second.
why_this_approach: Explosion readability depends on hierarchy: flash/core, body, debris, dust, mark.
Separating emitters makes timing and performance easier to tune than one all-purpose emitter.
Different renderers are chosen per layer: sprite for volume, mesh for chunks, decal for ground mark.
pros: Strong layer ownership and tuneability.
Supports size variants such as small/medium by scaling system parameters or emitter counts.
Renderer/material choices match the visual job.
cons: Many emitters increase maintenance cost.
Overdraw can spike from sprite body plus smoke/dust layers.
Authoring changes require understanding inter-emitter timing.
when_to_copy: Any one-shot impact with body, debris, dust, and lingering surface evidence.
when_to_avoid: Small hits that only need a flash and a few particles.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Explosion tot khong phai mot emitter that lon. No la dan nhac nho: flash doc nhan, body tao khoi, debris cho luc, dust cho moi truong, decal cho dau vet.

archetypes.intent: Create a looping smoke plume with controlled buoyancy, wind, base size, color, sprite growth, and soft volume material.
core_graph_or_stack: Emitter-level values define the plume personality: buoyancy, wind, and base size.
Particle spawn sets size, temperature, and initial position variation.
Particle update fades, moves, and kills puffs over their own lifetime.
Smoke material supplies atlas detail, normal/fake-lighting response, and depth fade.
why_this_approach: Smoke is a loop with organic variation; it benefits from particle-time curves and noise rather than pure burst logic.
Emitter-level controls make art direction faster because many particles inherit the same plume behavior.
Using a flipbook material gives smoke internal texture without simulating fluid volume.
pros: Reusable for chimney smoke, dust plumes, steam, and ambient fog wisps.
Clear split between emitter motion and material surface richness.
Good teaching example for particle time versus emitter-level controls.
cons: Sprite overdraw can be high in dense plumes.
Looping smoke exposes tiling and repeated flipbook frames if variation is weak.
Needs careful sorting and depth fade tuning.
when_to_copy: Looping smoke, steam, fog wisps, exhaust, ambient dust.
when_to_avoid: Sharp one-shot impact flashes or effects that need exact collision boundaries.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Smoke hay vi no duoc dieu khien boi nhieu hat song rieng. Emitter dat dieu kien chung nhu gio va buoyancy, con moi particle tu fade/grow theo tuoi cua no.

archetypes.intent: Drive boundary visuals from high-level user parameters such as color and dimensions instead of hardcoding each shape variant.
core_graph_or_stack: User.Color controls art direction from outside the system.
User.Dimensions makes the same concept fit multiple boundary sizes.
Decal and sparkle/support emitters separate surface boundary read from accent motion.
M_Mesh_Add/MI_Boundary_TechGrid supplies additive grid and height/noise masking.
why_this_approach: Boundary effects are often gameplay indicators; they should be data-driven by size and color.
A few high-level user params are safer than editing emitter internals for each placement.
Using one material family keeps box/cylinder/sphere variants visually coherent.
pros: Good Blueprint/Niagara contract.
Reusable across gameplay markers and environmental zones.
Easy to recolor or resize at runtime.
cons: If dimensions and material scale disagree, grid density may look inconsistent.
Emitter data may be inherited or missing in some variants, so tooling should handle parent/template patterns gracefully.
when_to_copy: Area of effect indicators, safe zones, capture zones, forcefield boundaries.
when_to_avoid: Pure cinematic effects where hand-authored shape timing matters more than runtime parameters.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Boundary la vi du hay ve User Parameters. BP hoac level chi nen noi 'mau gi, kich thuoc nao', con Niagara/material tu lo cach ve dep.

archetypes.intent: Represent pickup idle, spawn, success, timeout, and color variants with Niagara systems controlled by a gameplay Blueprint.
core_graph_or_stack: Idle system owns continuous attraction/readability.
Spawn, success, and timeout systems own state-transition moments.
Blueprint holds gameplay state, color choice, timeout/respawn, and system references.
Materials stay instance-based and color-tunable.
why_this_approach: Pickup effects need persistent affordance plus discrete feedback moments.
Separating state systems avoids making one Niagara graph responsible for all gameplay state.
User color parameters let the same visual structure represent buff, debuff, weapon, or player pickup classes.
pros: Clean runtime ownership: Blueprint controls state, Niagara controls look.
Easy to extend with new pickup categories.
Good user-parameter teaching case.
cons: More assets to keep synchronized.
State transitions can drift if Blueprint timing and Niagara lifetimes are not aligned.
Color-only variants may not be enough for very different item meanings.
when_to_copy: Pickups, interactables, buffs, timed rewards, collectible state effects.
when_to_avoid: One-off cinematic items where authored sequence timing is more important than reusable state.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Pickup nen tach idle va transition. Idle noi 'toi dang o day', success/timeout noi 'chuyen trang thai vua xay ra'. BP quan ly logic, Niagara quan ly cam giac.

archetypes.intent: Create a compact weapon flash from burst sprites, SubUV playback, dynamic material parameters, and a light renderer.
core_graph_or_stack: Burst spawns the flash instantly.
SubUV module chooses fast frame animation.
Dynamic Material Parameters bridge Niagara timing to material response.
Light renderer gives real scene flash separate from sprite emissive.
why_this_approach: Muzzle flashes are extremely short; they need immediate silhouette and light response.
A light renderer sells the event in the scene better than emissive alone.
Dynamic params keep the material reusable while Niagara controls per-shot variation.
pros: Very readable gameplay feedback.
Good separation of visual flash and scene illumination.
Reuses smoke/fire material family for pyro texture response.
cons: Light renderers can be expensive if fired rapidly by many weapons.
SubUV textures need good frame selection for a one-shot flash.
Too much emissive plus light can overexpose the shot.
when_to_copy: Rifle shots, launcher muzzle flashes, short magical casts, impact flashes needing scene light.
when_to_avoid: Sustained beams or loops where continuous light would be too costly.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Muzzle flash khong keo dai. No can bat len dung mot khoanh khac: burst, SubUV nhanh, light renderer, roi tat. Day la effect ve timing hon la ve graph phuc tap.

archetypes.intent: Trigger small surface-specific effects with a foot-side user parameter and layered flame/smoke/burst/decal style emitters.
core_graph_or_stack: User.RightFoot controls left/right placement or orientation logic.
Small burst layers give immediate contact feedback.
Smoke/flame layers carry residual visual read.
Footprint/decal layer leaves grounded evidence.
why_this_approach: Footsteps are frequent and gameplay-adjacent, so the system needs simple external control.
The effect must be small but layered enough to read as contact with a surface.
Separating residual smoke from contact burst makes the step feel less like a generic particle pop.
pros: Clear animation/BP to Niagara contract.
Scales to different surface types.
Good example of small layered VFX.
cons: Can become noisy if triggered too often.
Needs strict lifetime and spawn count control for performance.
Surface-specific variants need consistent naming and material reuse.
when_to_copy: Footsteps, landing puffs, small contact events, surface reaction VFX.
when_to_avoid: Large impacts where full explosion layering is more appropriate.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Footstep la effect nho nhung van co lop: tiep xuc, du am, dau vet. Hay dung user param de BP/animation noi chan nao dang cham dat.

archetypes.intent: Combine ribbon/electric Niagara with mesh overlay status material and Blueprint target management.
core_graph_or_stack: Blueprint manages target/attachment state.
Niagara ribbon or arc system owns electric connection visuals.
Mesh overlay material applies status read to affected meshes.
Boundary Niagara provides local area/interaction feedback.
why_this_approach: Status effects need gameplay awareness that should not live only inside Niagara.
Ribbons communicate connection; mesh overlay communicates affected target.
Separating boundary, ribbon, and overlay makes each layer legible.
pros: Good full-chain pattern from Blueprint to Niagara to Material.
Reusable for beams, shocks, buffs, debuffs, and linked-target effects.
Keeps target logic out of material graphs.
cons: More moving pieces than a simple emitter.
Requires careful runtime cleanup of looping impact and overlay state.
Ribbon/material timing must agree with Blueprint target changes.
when_to_copy: Electric links, tether spells, beam-to-target gameplay, status effects on actors.
when_to_avoid: Standalone visual-only loops that do not need target state.
archetypes.teaching_notes_vi: Tesla la bai hoc full chain: BP biet target, Niagara ve duong dien, material overlay cho thay ai dang bi anh huong. Moi lop co viec rieng.
